strengths: The paper addresses a timely and socially significant question: whether agentic multi-modal reasoning models (ChatGPT o3) with tool use and web access can perform fine-grained image geolocation that threatens user privacy.

The threat model—unwitting victims whose casual photos inadvertently reveal location—is more adversarial and realistic than prior benign landmark-based geolocation benchmarks, and is reasonably well motivated relative to existing work on VLM geolocation and privacy leakage.

The paper goes beyond pure capability evaluation: it categorizes the visual clues used by the model (street layout, front yard design, etc.) and conducts occlusion/masking experiments that provide some causal evidence about which cues drive accurate inference, hinting at mitigation strategies.

The qualitative example chats in the appendix are informative and illustrate the multi-step reasoning + web search process in detail, and the authors state they will not release the dataset for licensing/privacy reasons.
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scale and rigor: the entire study rests on only 50 images, with no statistical significance testing, no variance across runs, and no confidence analysis. Key headline claims (60% within 1 mile) are based on roughly 30 images.

Evidence of selection bias that undermines the central claim: the authors test four prompts and 'selected the inferred geolocation with the highest precision as final prediction.' This best-of-N cherry-picking inflates accuracy and is inconsistent with a realistic adversarial scenario where the attacker gets one shot. The paper also states its goal is 'to find the optimal image for privacy leakage analysis,' suggesting deliberate selection of the most geolocatable scenes rather than representative sampling.

The dataset is sourced from Google Street View, not actual user selfies/social media photos. Street View imagery is professionally captured with abundant, unusual geolocatable cues (this is essentially the GeoGuessr setting), so the claimed realism of the 'casual selfie' threat model is not actually tested. The paper conflates these two very different image distributions.

Internal inconsistencies raise concerns about experimental care: the dataset is described as 50 US images of individuals in front of private residences, yet the appendix includes Shanghai and Suzhou examples; the Figure 1 caption describes a 'private residence' while the image shows a state park hiking trail; the abstract claims 'front yard design' as a key cue while the figure reports 'Unique Design'; there is a reference to each image being paired with a 'fourth truth location.'

No baselines whatsoever: no comparison against GPT-4o, other VLMs, dedicated geolocation models (e.g., PIGEON/GeoCLIP), or a human baseline, making it impossible to contextualize whether the observed leakage is specific to agentic reasoning models with web access or a general capability.

The masking/occlusion 'experiments' are essentially case studies on 2–3 images presented as figures, not a systematic ablation across the dataset, so the causal claims about clue importance and defense feasibility are only weakly supported.

Reproducibility is poor: the dataset will not be released, the model is a closed-source black box whose behavior changes over time, and no prompts/protocol details are provided in a form sufficient for replication.

Ethical handling is incomplete: the appendix reproduces full transcripts that pinpoint exact street addresses of real locations, which itself constitutes a doxxing artifact; there is no IRB/ethics-board discussion, and the paper's dual-use value (a how-to for geolocation prompting) is not carefully weighed.

Novelty over the cited prior work on VLM geolocation inference (e.g., [15], [17]) is incremental; the main delta is a different image distribution, a single closed model, and prompt-based red-teaming rather than a new technique, dataset resource, or defense.

Writing quality is below the bar for a top-tier venue, with multiple typos and grammatical errors ('lveraging,' 'exsting,' 'defination,' 'Unite State,' 'adversial') and an empty/truncated appendix structure that suggests a rushed submission.

strengths: Timely and socially relevant topic: the privacy risk of agentic, tool-using reasoning models (ChatGPT o3) performing fine-grained image geolocation is an important and under-studied threat surface, and the paper is right that the o3/o4-mini system card discussion omits it.

The paper attempts a causal analysis rather than only correlational clue counting: the targeted occlusion/masking experiments (e.g., Figures 10-13) are a reasonable idea for probing which visual cues drive geolocation accuracy.
The clue taxonomy (Figure 14) categorizing visual cues into Building Features, Identification, Urban Infrastructure, etc., could be a useful artifact for future work on privacy-aware image sharing.
The paper is generally readable, and the qualitative chat traces in the appendix make the failure/success modes transparent.
weaknesses: Fundamental mismatch between the claimed threat model and the actual data: the paper motivates the study via attackers exploiting 'selfies casually posted on social media,' but all 50 images are sourced from Google Maps/Street View with blurred faces. Street View is exactly the corpus o3's web-search tools can retrieve and match against, so the reported 60% street-level accuracy may largely reflect retrieval of the source imagery rather than inference from 'inadvertent micro-cues' — the central claim is therefore not convincingly supported. This confound is never addressed or controlled for.

Severe evaluation weaknesses: (a) only 50 images, with no confidence intervals or statistical treatment; (b) only one model (o3) is tested — no baselines such as GPT-4o, Gemini, Claude, or prior geolocation systems (e.g., PIGEON/GeoCLIP), and no human-expert baseline, so there is no way to judge whether o3's capability is exceptional; (c) no repeated runs, despite o3's known output non-determinism.

Cherry-picking of prompts: the authors tested four prompts and explicitly 'selected the inferred geolocation with the highest precision as final prediction' (Section 4.1 / Figure 3). Reporting the best-of-4 result as the headline 60% figure is methodologically invalid and inflates the risk claim; per-prompt results are never reported.

The occlusion/causal analysis is anecdotal: conclusions about 'street layout and front yard design' being key cues are drawn from frequency counts of self-reported reasoning plus a handful of single-image masking case studies, with no systematic quantification across the dataset (e.g., masking each clue category over all 50 images and measuring accuracy deltas). The authors themselves concede the clues are 'interdependent,' which further undermines the cue-importance claims.

The novelty claim of being 'the first' is overstated: the paper itself cites prior work evaluating precise geolocation inference of VLMs ([15], [16], [17]) and private attribute inference ([29]); the incremental contribution is essentially the tool-using o3 setting plus a small self-made dataset. The OpenAI system card and public discussion already flag o3's geolocation risk.

Internal inconsistencies undermine credibility: Figure 1's caption describes a 'private residence' but the figure shows a State Park hiking trail; the dataset is described as non-landmark, privacy-relevant residential scenes, yet several appendix examples are famous landmarks (Disneyland Shanghai, Clearwater Beach, Loon Mountain); 'a fourth truth location' (p.2), 'lveraging', 'exsting', 'Urban Planing', 'Defination' and other errors indicate a rushed manuscript.
No defense or mitigation is actually proposed or evaluated; the paper stops at 'masking critical features reduces accuracy' — an intuitive result — and offers only speculative suggestions.

Reproducibility is very limited: the dataset will not be released (licensing), the tested model is closed and evolving, and the prompting/selection protocol is not precisely specified enough to replicate the numbers.

Dual-use concerns are not carefully handled: the paper effectively provides a validated recipe (prompt templates + image selection criteria) for doxxing via o3, without an ethics statement or discussion of responsible disclosure to OpenAI.

strengths: Timely and socially relevant topic: privacy leakage from agentic multimodal reasoning models (e.g., ChatGPT o3 with web-search tool use) is an important and under-examined threat surface, and the paper draws attention to it at the right moment.

The paper goes beyond a single anecdote: it attempts a quantitative evaluation (distance-to-ground-truth distribution), a manual taxonomy of visual cues (Figure 14), and targeted occlusion/masking experiments to provide causal evidence about which features drive inference success.

The masking experiments (Figures 10-13) are a nice touch, showing both that removing a key clue degrades accuracy and that o3 can fall back on secondary cues -- this has direct implications for potential defense design.
Reasonable related-work positioning distinguishing inference-time privacy exploitation from training-data leakage and jailbreak research.
weaknesses: Fundamental mismatch between the stated threat model and the actual data. The paper claims to study 'realistic, privacy-sensitive scenarios' of users 'casually upload[ing] selfies' with privacy-relevant backgrounds, and the dataset is described as 50 US images of 'identifiable individuals in front of private residences' (NY, LA, SF, Boston, Columbus). However, images are sourced from Google Street View with blurred faces, and the appendix examples are tourist landmarks (Disneyland Shanghai, Clearwater Beach, Loon Mountain, Dushu Lake Church), including locations in China, not US private residences. Figure 1's caption describes a 'private residence' but the example is a state-park hiking trail. This inconsistency undermines the central realism claim.

Severe evaluation bias from prompt selection: the authors tested four prompts and 'selected the inferred geolocation with the highest precision as final prediction' (Section 4.1/Figure 3). This best-of-4 selection inflates the headline 60% street-level accuracy; a per-prompt or fixed-prompt protocol is required for an unbiased estimate. No variance across prompts or repeated runs of the (stochastic) model is reported.

Very small dataset (50 images) with no statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, no significance tests, and apparently inconsistent counts (Figure 6 sums to 52, not 50). Conclusions about 60%/84% thresholds rest on ~30 samples.

No baselines or comparisons whatsoever: no evaluation of other models (GPT-4o, Gemini, Claude, open-source VLMs), no human-baseline comparison (the claim that o3 exceeds 'non-expert human inspectors' is asserted, not measured), and no comparison to prior geolocation systems such as PIGEON, despite claims of a 'first systematic study.' The novelty claim is weakened by prior work the authors themselves cite ([15], [16], [17]) on VLM geolocation privacy.

Clue analysis is subjective and manual: cue categories were presumably assigned by the authors from reading o3's reasoning traces, with no inter-annotator agreement or validation; frequency counts (Figures 4-5) cannot establish which cues 'significantly contribute' to success -- the paper even admits the interdependence of cues makes this 'challenging.' The causal masking evidence is anecdotal (roughly two mask/unmask pairs in the appendix).

Reproducibility is essentially impossible: the dataset will not be released (licensing), no code or prompts pipeline is released, and the subject is a closed-source, silently-updated commercial model. The formal notation in Section 3.1 (a factorized autoregressive likelihood) adds no technical content.

The paper is very short on substance for a top-tier venue: roughly 5 pages including figures, with a lightweight methodology, four qualitative appendix chats, and an effectively empty methodological contribution. It reads as a workshop-style audit note rather than a full research paper.

Quality and consistency issues throughout: numerous typos ('lveraging,' 'exsting,' 'adversial,' 'Data Anotation,' 'Unite State,' 'fourth truth location,' 'Defination'), a mismatched Figure 1 caption, and missing ethical discussion details (e.g., no responsible disclosure to OpenAI, limited dual-use mitigation beyond stating that images are authorized/blurred).

strengths: Timely and socially significant problem: the paper identifies an under-explored inference-time privacy threat (image geolocation leakage / doxing) for multimodal reasoning models, which is highly relevant to AI safety and privacy communities.

DOXBENCH is a genuinely useful contribution: 500 real-world, high-resolution, EXIF-annotated images with a three-level privacy risk taxonomy (including a novel 'Mirror'/reflection category), directly addressing the acknowledged limitations of prior benchmarks built on Street View or landmark images.

Comprehensive evaluation across 11 closed- and open-source models, with a well-designed, objective evaluation pipeline (geocoding to GPS, Census Bureau hierarchical accuracy at state/metro/tract/block levels) that improves on prior fuzzy LLM-judge based accuracy measures.

The root-cause analysis is substantive rather than superficial: human and LLM-as-judge validation of clue-based reasoning, CoT prompting transfer experiments showing MLLMs can be elevated toward MLRM geolocation ability, tool-augmented analysis, and mirror-case analysis collectively support the two claimed causal factors.

The defense section is unusually thorough for an attack paper, including Gaussian-noise perturbation with mechanistic failure analysis, prompt-based defenses with utility trade-offs, and the finding that Llama Guard 4 labels everything safe.
The information-theoretic GLARE metric (mutual information formulation, spherical-cap vs flat-disk error analysis in the appendix) shows technical care and is a reusable measurement contribution.
weaknesses: Severe geographic bias: all 500 images come from six California regions. Models' world knowledge of California is disproportionately rich, so reported absolute leakage levels may substantially overestimate global risk; there is no cross-region or cross-country validation, undermining the generality of the central claims.

The human-model comparison is weak: only 5 undergraduate participants and 30 images. Claims that models are '15–21× better' than non-expert humans rest on a very small, unrepresentative sample without statistical significance testing or error bars.

GLARE's soundness is questionable: the 'risk term' H(R) is presented as if answering itself always leaks information, which conflates refusal behavior with leakage; the uniform-prior-over-Earth assumption conflicts with a California-only test distribution; the geometric mean of median and mean error is heuristic. Table 1 anomalies (e.g., GPT-4o vanilla VRR 12.95% but AED 2.01 km; GLARE rising while AED worsens under CoT) suggest the metric's behavior needs more careful justification.

Internal inconsistencies in data collection description (Section 1 says images 'captured during real driving sessions', Section 3.2 describes staged scenes, posing, and recreated celebrity incidents), and the abstract's claim of 'first' structured framework overlooks concurrent works the paper itself cites ([21], [22], [3]).

Several experiments are small and potentially cherry-picked: the tool-augmentation study uses only 10 sampled failure cases per risk tier with manual selection of 'challenging' cases; the reasoning-pattern study uses 30 samples; no confidence intervals are reported anywhere. IQR outlier filtering is mentioned but not justified or applied consistently.

Dual-use/ethics concerns: the paper provides concrete prompts and procedures that lower the barrier to doxing, releases a benchmark of high-resolution geolocatable images (including staged selfies of identifiable researchers), and recreates a real stalking case; the ethical statement is present but brief, and no discussion of responsible release (e.g., blurred faces, withheld GPS, red-teamed access) is given.
The defense evaluation covers only three models, and the GEOMINER/CLUEMINER frameworks are essentially prompt-engineering pipelines whose novelty relative to the CoT experiments is incremental.

strengths: Timely and socially relevant topic: inference-time geolocation privacy leakage from user-generated images is an underexamined risk surface for MLRMs, and the paper raises awareness with concrete numbers.

Broad empirical coverage: evaluation of 11 models (closed- and open-source) with a structured, multi-granularity metric suite (state/metro/tract/block accuracy, error distances, and the proposed GLARE metric).

Several thoughtful components: the tiered Visual Privacy Risk Framework, the mirror/reflection category reproducing a real-world incident, the analysis of tool-augmented O3, and the defense discussion (perturbation, prompt-based, Llama Guard 4) which shows current guardrails fail to detect this risk.
The dataset contains EXIF ground truth, enabling fine-grained distance-based evaluation rather than coarse city-level matching used in prior work.
weaknesses: Limited novelty and positioning: the core observation (VLMs/MLRMs can geolocate images and this is a privacy risk) is already established by concurrent works the paper itself cites ([3], [21], [22]). The delta is essentially a California-specific dataset and prompting variants (CoT, two-stage 'GEOMINER'), which are incremental engineering rather than a new insight or method.

Geographic bias fundamentally undermines validity: all 500 images come from six California cities. State-level accuracy of ~100% is trivially expected, and models may exploit geographic priors or training-data memorization of California (e.g., Street View-derived knowledge) rather than genuine clue-based reasoning. The paper's central claim that 'clue-based reasoning' drives leakage is supported only by 30 cherry-picked samples (those where the model was already correct at metro level) judged by 3 annotators and GPT-4o — a very weak evidentiary base.

GLARE metric is ad hoc: combining Shannon entropy of the answer/refusal event with log(A0/(pi*d50*d_bar)) using the geometric mean of median and mean error has no clear information-theoretic justification despite the mutual-information framing in Appendix C; the two terms are not actually mutual information quantities, and the composite is hard to interpret or compare.

Statistical rigor is lacking: outlier filtering with IQR on error distances discards exactly the heavy-tail failures that matter most for privacy risk assessment; no confidence intervals, no variance across API runs despite known nondeterminism of commercial APIs; the tool-augmented O3 experiment uses only 10 manually sampled cases per tier.

Human comparison is inadequate: 5 undergraduate participants on 30 images with a 300-second limit cannot establish the claimed '21x lower error' conclusion at any statistical standard; no expert (e.g., GeoGuessr-proficient) baseline, no within-subject design details, no IRB approval mentioned (only 'internal review').

Significant ethical concerns insufficiently addressed: the dataset includes GPS coordinates of private residences, license plates, house numbers, and staged scenes with researchers posing; responsible disclosure to model providers is not mentioned; plans for dataset release (with exact coordinates of 'privacy spaces') are dual-use and not discussed. No IRB review is reported for the human study.

Writing and internal consistency problems: Section 4.3 contains an incoherent claim ('models ... demonstrate weak robustness ... and effectively narrow the query scope' — this appears to say the opposite of the intended finding); 'we implemented one prompt variants'; Figure 3's pie chart labels are garbled; the abstract claims models predict 'the address and GPS coordinates' while results show mostly metropolitan-level accuracy.

Defenses are preliminary and somewhat off-topic: Gaussian noise and a system prompt are known-weak baselines, and the Llama Guard 4 'failure' is a single negative result with limited analysis of why or how guardrails should be adapted.

Threat-model framing is overbroad: the paper claims 'novel attack framework' (GEOMINER), but it is a simple two-prompt pipeline where one MLLM describes clues for another; this does not constitute a methodological contribution commensurate with top-tier standards.
Dataset scale (500 images, single U.S. state, single device/iPhone 14 Pro) limits ecological validity and generalizability of conclusions about 'real-world' social media leakage.

strengths: Timely and societally relevant topic: location-related privacy leakage from user-generated images via multi-modal reasoning models is an under-explored threat, and the paper is well positioned relative to concurrent geolocation-privacy work.

DOXBENCH is a genuinely useful contribution: 500 high-resolution, self-captured images with EXIF ground truth, annotated with a three-level privacy risk framework, explicitly targeting private/semi-private spaces that prior Street View / landmark-based datasets miss.

Broad systematic evaluation across 11 models (closed- and open-source MLRMs and MLLMs), with a sensible multi-granularity accuracy protocol (state / metro / census tract / block) rather than fuzzy LLM-judge matching.

The analysis chain is coherent: evidence for clue-based reasoning (human + LLM-judge), CoT prompting to instill the pattern in MLLMs, CLUEMINER for categorizing exploited clues, tool-augmented O3 experiments, and mirror/reflection cases — collectively supporting the two claimed causal factors.

Useful negative results on defenses: Gaussian-noise perturbations are inconsistent and mechanism-dependent, prompt-based defenses trade off utility, and Llama Guard 4 fails entirely on this threat class, motivating privacy-alignment as future work.
Ethical statement is present and the dataset collection (researchers' own staged photos) avoids third-party privacy harms.
weaknesses: Apparent inconsistency in the headline GLARE metric: with A0 = 1.48e8 km^2 and log2 area ratios, the leakage term should be bounded by roughly 47 bits even for near-perfect pinpointing, yet reported GLARE values reach 2000+ bits. The derivation in Appendix C (geometric mean of d50 and mean d, unit handling) does not obviously reproduce the reported numbers, and sqrt(median*mean) is not the geometric mean of the error distribution. This numerical inconsistency in the paper's central metric must be clarified or corrected.

The human-model comparison (Section 7) rests on only 5 undergraduate participants and 30 images. Claims such as '15–21x better AED' and 'up to 21x lower error' are statistically fragile at this sample size; no variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing is reported anywhere in the paper.

Geographic bias: all 500 images were captured in six California cities by the authors. Models may have disproportionate training coverage of California, inflating apparent leakage; generalization to other regions/countries is not tested, weakening the 'real-world threat' claim.

Outlier filtering with IQR on error distances is applied to the main results table, which directly benefits models with heavy-tailed error distributions and may overstate geolocation accuracy; the filtering policy is not justified per-model.

Novelty is partly incremental relative to concurrent works (e.g., arXiv 2502.11163, 2502.14412, 2408.09474): the core observation that VLMs perform image geolocation is known; the contributions are a more privacy-sensitive dataset, an analysis, and a metric — so 'first to explicitly define' claims should be softened.

CLUEMINER and several evaluations depend on LLM-based components (O4-mini analyzer, GPT-4o judge, LLM classifier) without validation of the categorization quality, raising reliability and reproducibility concerns; details on dataset release and exact evaluation harness are thin.

Small-N sub-analyses: mirror-case analysis uses 46 images (top-6 models only) and tool-use comparison uses 10 sampled failure cases per tier, making the strong conclusions ('tools increase risk', 'O3 most accurate on reflections') under-supported.

Writing quality is below top-venue standards: numerous grammatical errors ('one prompt variants', 'We will detail introduce', 'These models frequently make use of these visual clues, yet they' capitalized mid-sentence), inconsistent figure/table references (Figure 3 cited for sampling locations but showing distribution), and a generally discussion-style defense section (Section 8) with limited evaluation depth (3 models, VRR only).
